title: India and ADB sign $230 million loan to modernise water supply and sanitation in Chennai
subtitle:
Chennai Climate-Resilient Water Security and Sewerage Project will help strengthen city’s resilience to climate change, improve public health and quality of life, and support a more efficient and financially sustainable urban water system
In line with Government of India’s flagship urban development interventions under Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation 2.0 and Urban Challenge Fund, ADB’s latest investment builds on earlier projects in Chennai to expand access to safe and equitable water and waste management services
body_text:
The Government of India and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) today signed a $230 million loan to modernise and expand Chennai’s water supply and sanitation infrastructure.
The Government of India’s engagement with ADB for the finalisation of the loan was done under the guidance of Shri Baldeo Purushartha, Joint Secretary (ADB & Japan), Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), Ministry of Finance.
Accordingly, the loan documents were signed by Shri Saurabh Singh, Deputy Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance, on behalf of the Government of India, and Ms. Mio Oka, Country Director, India Resident Mission on behalf of the ADB.
The Chennai Climate-Resilient Water Security and Sewerage Project will improve access to safe and reliable water supply and better sanitation services across Chennai. It will also help strengthen the city’s resilience to climate change, improve public health and quality of life, and support a more efficient and financially sustainable urban water system.
ADB’s latest investment builds on earlier projects in the city to expand access to safe and equitable water and waste management services, in line with the Government of India’s flagship urban development interventions, such as the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation 2.0 and the Urban Challenge Fund.
The project will construct over 170 km of water supply pipes and sewer pipes, upgrade seven water pumping stations and 38 sewer pumping stations, and strengthen water utility assets and operations management through performance-based contracts. With this, Chennai will become the first Indian city to implement a comprehensive ring-main solution, a closed-loop plumbing system designed to maintain balanced water pressure and deliver water efficiently across service areas, improving reliability, equity, and resilience to natural hazards in its urban water supply system.
ADB will help digitally transform water and sanitation services through real-time monitoring, data-driven decision-making, and improved customer responsiveness. The project will introduce advanced technologies to eliminate hazardous manual sewer inspections, make blockage detection faster and safer, enhance worker safety, and prepare distribution networks in at least two Greater Chennai zones for future investments.

enrichment.summary: India and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) signed a $230 million loan agreement to fund the Chennai Climate-Resilient Water Security and Sewerage Project, aimed at modernising the city's water supply and sanitation infrastructure. The project will lay over 170 km of water and sewer pipes, upgrade 7 water and 38 sewer pumping stations, and make Chennai the first Indian city to implement a comprehensive ring-main water distribution system. It also includes digital monitoring tools and technology to eliminate hazardous manual sewer inspections.
enrichment.context:
This loan builds on ADB's earlier engagements in Chennai's water and sanitation sector and is positioned within the Government of India's broader urban development agenda, including AMRUT 2.0 (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), which focuses on universal water supply coverage and sewerage/septage management in cities, and the newer Urban Challenge Fund aimed at incentivising urban infrastructure reforms. Chennai has historically faced acute water stress, alternating between severe droughts (as seen in 2019) and flooding, making climate-resilient water infrastructure a priority for the city's long-term sustainability.

ADB has been a long-standing multilateral partner for India's urban infrastructure financing, often structuring loans around performance-based contracts to improve utility efficiency and financial sustainability alongside physical infrastructure creation. The introduction of a ring-main system and digital, real-time monitoring reflects a shift toward technologically advanced, equity-focused urban water management, which could serve as a template for other Indian cities facing similar water security and sanitation worker safety challenges.

prelims_questions.question: The 'ring-main solution' mentioned in the context of Chennai's new water project refers to which of the following?
options: A system of underground reservoirs for rainwater harvesting
A closed-loop plumbing system that maintains balanced water pressure across a distribution network
A method of desalinating seawater for urban supply
prelims_questions.explanation: The release describes the ring-main system as a closed-loop plumbing system designed to maintain balanced water pressure and deliver water efficiently, improving reliability and equity.

prelims_questions.question: The Chennai Climate-Resilient Water Security and Sewerage Project is being financed through a loan from which institution?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that India and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) signed the $230 million loan for this project.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of multilateral development bank financing, such as ADB loans, in addressing urban water and sanitation infrastructure gaps in India. Illustrate with reference to recent initiatives.
Examine how climate-resilient urban water management systems can help Indian cities cope with the dual challenges of water scarcity and flooding.

study_notes.reason: The release carries a testable factual core (ADB loan amount, AMRUT 2.0, ring-main system as a first-in-India feature) alongside genuine analytical material on climate resilience, urban water governance and manual scavenging elimination, making it moderately balanced though not deeply substantive.
